Hi! I’m a first-year MA Economics student at Duke University currently studying microeconomics, econometrics and game theory. My interests are broad — economics, ethics, politics, the rapid rise of AI — and in the past year I’ve done research on YIMBY housing policy, population ethics and global warming. Outside of work, I enjoy a good book or TV show, playing guitar (electric and acoustic) and (very slowly) lowering my handicap on the golf course.

title: Wesley Stone
text:
Biography
I was born in Madison, Wisconsin, but I’d lived in Atlanta, Georgia nearly my entire life before returning to my Midwestern roots for college. I became interested in philosophy my first semester after taking an ethics class, and I soon decided to add data science to explore the foundations of the machine learning and artificial intelligence technology taking the world by storm. After studying abroad in Amsterdam junior spring, I spent my senior year immersed in research capstones for my two majors. For data science, I worked with a group to study the behavior of the Portland housing market after a statewide ban on exclusive single-family zoning. Our final paper is accessible on my website. And my philosophy capstone, entitled “A Risk-Sensitive Approach to Population Ethics,” takes on the difficult question of determining a social welfare function to measure the value of populations of varying sizes and quality of life. I published this paper in the journal Dianoia, and presented my findings at a conference at Boston College. This summer, I returned to my role as an analyst at Georgia Tech’s Urban Climate Lab, contributing to critical research on warming trends in the biggest US cities. Now I’m beginning my career as a Blue Devil and diving deep into the world of economics, as well as beginning to construct a vision of what the future looks like for me.

title: Human Heat Tolerance Index
text: At a wet bulb (humidity-adjusted) temperature of 87°F, studies have shown that healthy young adults are at risk for severe symptoms with prolonged exposure. If this threshold were to be breached with any regularity, it would have profound implications for the way we could live our lives outdoors. For instance, municipal services, such as garbage collection, might have to be reduced or suspended in such a scenario. As such, Georgia Tech’s Urban Climate Lab set out to answer the obvious question: when may this critical limit be reached? I assisted the Urban Climate Lab in acquiring, cleaning and wrangling the data for the Human Heat Tolerance Index, which tracks wet bulb temperatures in the 25 largest cities in the US. According to the analysis, over a dozen major metropolises may be at risk of threshold heat events within the decade.

title: Extreme Wet-Bulb Temperatures Across U.S. Cities
text:
→ Open the interactive map · source on GitHub



Wet-bulb temperature — what a thermometer reads when wrapped in a wet cloth — folds humidity into the reading, and it is the number that actually governs whether the human body can shed heat. Past a critical wet-bulb value, sweat stops evaporating fast enough and core temperature climbs without limit. This project maps how close 56 U.S. cities have come to that limit.
Building on my work with Georgia Tech’s Urban Climate Lab on the Human Heat Tolerance Index, I pulled two decades of hourly NOAA NCEI Local Climatological Data — 2005 through 2025, one primary airport station per city — and extracted each city’s hottest wet-bulb hour of every year, along with the dry-bulb temperature, relative humidity and dew point that accompanied it. The result is an interactive D3 map: hover a city for its record peak, its warming trend and a projection toward its critical threshold; click for year-by-year detail with fitted trends.

What it shows
The threshold follows the 2022 Penn State study (Vecellio et al., Journal of Applied Physiology), which tested the long-assumed 35 °C limit and found the real ceiling for healthy young adults is closer to 31 °C (~87 °F) in humid conditions — and lower still, about 28 °C (~82 °F), in dry heat, where danger arrives through extreme dry-bulb temperature at low humidity. The map applies both, sorting cities into humid and arid regimes.
Two arguments run through the piece. The first is about what the number would actually mean: 87 °F wet-bulb is not the point at which heat becomes unpleasant, it is the point at which a healthy adult doing almost nothing can no longer hold core temperature steady — so outdoor construction, trash collection, school sports, delivery work and emergency response all become unsafe well before it. The second is about how to read a trend line. The fitted slopes are noisy and mostly point past 2100, which invites the wrong conclusion. But these are annual maxima — spikes, not plateaus — and a threshold is crossed by a single hour, not an average year. Yearly peaks scatter about 1.4 °F around their own trend lines, every one of the 56 cities has recorded a peak above its current trend value, 23 are already within 3 °F of their threshold, and Phoenix has touched its 82 °F arid line. As the line rises beneath a scatter that stays just as wide, the odds of one dangerous hour climb far faster than any “projected year” suggests.


Method notes

Data: NOAA NCEI LCD hourly FM-15 observations, 2005–2025, cleaned and concatenated per city.
Trends: OLS slope of annual maxima against year, reported per decade with R². These fits are deliberately presented as illustrations of a current slope rather than forecasts — the R² values are low because year-to-year variation dwarfs the long-term signal.
Built with: R for the data pipeline, D3 and TopoJSON for the map. The site is a single self-contained HTML file with the city data and U.S. geometry inlined.

title: Network Analysis of Bad Movies
text:
In this project we performed a network analysis of bad movies, defined as having an IMDB rating of 2/10 or less and at least 10 total ratings. From an initial dataset of 86,000 this left us 871 total films. To create our networks, we scraped cast and crew data, and used the built-in genre variable, giving us two different lenses to peer through. From the personnel perspective, we did not find large communities of people involved with multiple films, but rather isolated clusters involved in one or two, suggesting that most bad movies are the product of random variation over time rather than coming from a core set of bad actors and directors. Our genre analysis did observe several distinct communities, which led us to conclude that bad movies are often a failed combination of action, horror and sci-fi.

title: Self-Replicating Robots in Minecraft
text:
In this project, we created self-replicating robots in Minecraft, prioritizing independence and resilience against unexpected circumstances. We used turtles from the mod CC: Tweaked. A self-replicating turtle successfully gathers non-renewable resources from the environment and grows renewable resources from a limited starting supply. It then crafts those resources into a copy of itself, equips that copy with the necessary tools to self-replicate, and releases that copy into the world. We limited the scope of our project to ignore fuel consumption by the turtles, as well as continuity between loaded and unloaded parts of the world. At known critical points, the program has an estimated failure rate of 4.4%. Our program demonstrates the power of hard-coded environment-agnostic behaviors as part of a complex AI system interacting with an unknown, highly variable environment.

title: A Risk-Sensitive Approach to Population Ethics
text:
My philosophy capstone project was in the field of population ethics, defined by the Oxford Handbook of Population Ethics as “the investigation of various ethical issues that arise when we consider how our actions affect both who is born and how many people are born.” Below is the abstract of “A Risk-Sensitive Approach to Population Ethics”, and if interested, you can find the full paper here.
Is it better if more (or fewer) people live? Is it better to make people happy than to make happy people? How many people should there ever be? Answering these questions could help inform important decisions impacting the number of people in existence, from an individual’s decision to have children to a government’s decision to implement “natalist” policies to even a worldwide decision to colonize other planets in the not-too-distant future. Philosophers in the field of population ethics have taken on this weighty project, but have been stuck for decades on the dilemma posed by the “Repugnant Conclusion,” which there are many very compelling arguments for, but which also seems intuitively unacceptable. I argue that we can have our cake and eat it too if we recognize a key difference between abstract thought experiments and real-world decisions: while we can operate with certainty in the former, the latter involves considerable uncertainty, and the risk of something going badly wrong must be taken into account. My proposed “risk-sensitive” approach aims to preserve the theoretical strength of the Repugnant Conclusion while limiting the unintuitive consequences of accepting it, and, if successful in doing so, perhaps illuminates a way forward for the field.
